question.title: Auto Scaling Health Checks
question.scenario: An application runs on EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer with Auto Scaling. The instances occasionally become unresponsive due to application issues but the EC2 status checks pass. The Auto Scaling group is not replacing these unhealthy instances.
question.question-text: What should be configured to ensure Auto Scaling replaces instances that fail ALB health checks?

choices.choice: Increase the EC2 health check grace period
Enable ELB health checks for the Auto Scaling group
Configure CloudWatch alarms for CPU utilization
Enable detailed monitoring on EC2 instances

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: By default, Auto Scaling only checks whether the instance is running. Think about what additional health signal the load balancer could provide.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: By default, Auto Scaling groups only use EC2 health checks, which verify the instance is running. To replace instances that fail Application Load Balancer health checks (application-level issues), you must explicitly enable ELB health checks for the Auto Scaling group. When enabled, an instance is considered unhealthy if either EC2 status checks OR ELB health checks fail.

ul.li: Health check grace period prevents terminating instances during startup before the application is ready.
Custom health checks can be implemented using SetInstanceHealth API.
Instances marked unhealthy are terminated and replaced, not rebooted.

question.title: Decoupling with SQS
question.scenario: A web application processes image uploads. The processing takes several minutes and causes timeouts when handled synchronously. The architecture needs to decouple the upload acceptance from the processing to improve reliability.
question.question-text: Which architecture pattern using AWS services would best decouple the image upload acceptance from processing?

choices.choice: Use larger EC2 instances to process images faster
Increase the timeout on the web server to allow longer processing times
Add more web servers behind the load balancer
Store uploads in S3, send messages to SQS, and have worker instances process from the queue

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about how a message queue between the upload tier and processing tier lets you accept work immediately and handle it later.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Decoupling the upload acceptance from processing using SQS is the best approach. The web tier accepts uploads (stores images in S3), sends a message to SQS with the image location, and immediately responds to the user. Worker instances poll SQS and process images asynchronously. This pattern improves reliability (processing failures don't lose uploads), scalability (workers scale independently), and user experience (no timeouts).

ul.li: S3 Event Notifications can trigger SQS messages automatically when objects are uploaded.
Dead-letter queues capture messages that fail processing repeatedly for debugging.
Visibility timeout should exceed the maximum processing time to prevent duplicate processing.

question.title: CloudFront Caching
question.scenario: A company hosts a website on EC2 instances in us-east-1. Users in Europe and Asia experience high latency when loading static content like images, CSS, and JavaScript files.
question.question-text: Which solution will most effectively reduce latency for global users?

choices.choice: Deploy Amazon CloudFront with the EC2 origin and enable caching for static content
Deploy additional EC2 instances in European and Asian Regions
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for static files
Increase EC2 instance sizes for better performance

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which AWS service uses a worldwide network of edge locations to serve cached content closer to end users.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Amazon CloudFront is a CDN that caches content at edge locations globally. When users request content, CloudFront serves it from the nearest edge location, dramatically reducing latency. For static content (images, CSS, JS), cache hit rates can be very high, meaning most requests never reach the origin. This provides both performance improvement and cost reduction (less origin load).

ul.li: Cache behaviors control which paths are cached and for how long (TTL settings).
Origin Shield adds a centralized caching layer to further reduce origin load.
CloudFront can also accelerate dynamic content by maintaining persistent connections to origins.

question.title: DynamoDB Capacity Modes
question.scenario: A mobile application has unpredictable traffic patterns with occasional viral spikes that are 10x normal load. The current provisioned capacity often results in throttling during spikes or wasted capacity during quiet periods.
question.question-text: Which DynamoDB capacity mode should be used to handle unpredictable workloads?

choices.choice: Provisioned capacity with auto scaling
On-demand capacity mode
Provisioned capacity with reserved capacity
DAX caching layer

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which DynamoDB billing mode removes the need to pre-provision capacity and handles sudden traffic spikes instantly.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode is ideal for unpredictable workloads. It automatically accommodates traffic as it rises and falls, instantly handling spikes without throttling. You pay per request rather than provisioning capacity. While on-demand has a higher per-request cost than well-utilized provisioned capacity, it eliminates throttling and wasted capacity for variable workloads.

ul.li: On-demand can handle up to double the previous peak traffic instantly; larger increases scale over 30 minutes.
Provisioned with auto scaling has a delay (typically minutes) to scale, which may cause throttling during sudden spikes.
Tables can be switched between modes once every 24 hours.

question.title: Read Replicas for Read Scaling
question.scenario: An RDS PostgreSQL database is experiencing high read traffic that's affecting write performance. The application has a 70% read to 30% write ratio.
question.question-text: Which solution scales read capacity while maintaining write performance on the primary?

choices.choice: Increase the instance size of the primary
Enable Multi-AZ deployment
Create Read Replicas and direct read traffic to them
Enable storage auto scaling

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about creating additional database copies that can serve read traffic, freeing the primary to focus on writes.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: RDS Read Replicas allow you to scale read capacity by creating copies of the primary database that can serve read traffic. Applications direct read queries to replicas while writes go to the primary. This offloads the primary, improving write performance. You can create up to 5 Read Replicas (15 for Aurora) within the same Region or across Regions.

ul.li: Read Replicas use asynchronous replication, so there's slight lag (typically milliseconds to seconds).
Applications must handle read-after-write consistency requirements if they read from replicas immediately after writing.
Read Replicas can be promoted to standalone databases for disaster recovery.

question.title: Reserved Instance Planning
question.scenario: A company has several production EC2 instances that run 24/7. Their AWS bill shows significant costs for On-Demand instances. They want to reduce compute costs for these stable, predictable workloads.
question.question-text: Which purchasing option provides the most cost savings for steady-state, predictable EC2 usage?

choices.choice: Dedicated Hosts
Spot Instances
On-Demand Instances with larger instance types
Reserved Instances or Savings Plans with 1 or 3-year commitment

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: For workloads that run around the clock with predictable capacity, consider which purchasing model trades a time commitment for a steep discount.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Reserved Instances and Compute Savings Plans offer significant discounts (up to 72%) compared to On-Demand pricing in exchange for committing to 1 or 3 years of usage. They're ideal for steady-state workloads with predictable capacity needs. Savings Plans offer more flexibility (apply across instance families and Regions) while Reserved Instances are more specific but can provide slightly better rates.

ul.li: All Upfront payment provides the maximum discount; No Upfront has the smallest discount.
Convertible RIs/Savings Plans allow changing instance types but have smaller discounts than Standard.
Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2, Fargate, and Lambda usage.

question.title: Data Transfer Costs
question.scenario: An application in us-east-1 frequently transfers large amounts of data to users worldwide. The AWS bill shows significant data transfer costs.
question.question-text: Which approach can reduce data transfer costs for global content delivery?

choices.choice: Transfer data during off-peak hours
Use CloudFront to cache and serve content from edge locations
Compress data before transfer
Use larger EC2 instances

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about how serving content from edge locations closer to users can also reduce the per-GB data transfer cost compared to origin egress.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: CloudFront can reduce data transfer costs in two ways: First, data transfer from CloudFront edge locations to users is less expensive per GB than transfer directly from EC2 or S3. Second, caching reduces the amount of data transferred from the origin. For frequently accessed content, the combination of lower per-GB costs and caching can significantly reduce total data transfer costs.

ul.li: CloudFront to origin transfer within AWS is free for data from S3 and cheaper for EC2 origins.
CloudFront Price Classes let you limit distribution to lower-cost regions.
S3 to CloudFront transfer is free; CloudFront to users is billed at CDN rates.

question.title: NAT Gateway vs NAT Instance
question.scenario: A company is reviewing costs for their private subnet instances to access the internet. They currently use NAT Gateway but are considering alternatives due to high data processing charges.
question.question-text: What is the cost characteristic difference between NAT Gateway and NAT Instance?

choices.choice: NAT Gateway has no data processing fees
NAT Gateway has hourly charges plus data processing fees; NAT Instance has only EC2 instance costs
Both have identical pricing structures
NAT Instance is always more expensive than NAT Gateway

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Compare the pricing models: one option has an hourly fee plus per-GB data processing charges; the other uses only standard compute costs.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: NAT Gateway has two cost components: hourly charges for the gateway itself plus data processing fees per GB of data processed. NAT Instance (running on EC2) has only standard EC2 instance costs with no additional data processing fees. For high data transfer volumes, NAT Instance can be more cost-effective, though it requires more management and may have lower bandwidth limits.

ul.li: NAT Gateway automatically scales up to 100 Gbps; NAT Instance depends on instance type.
NAT Gateway is managed and highly available in an AZ; NAT Instance requires manual HA setup.
For cost optimization, minimize data through NAT by using VPC endpoints for AWS service traffic.
